set.seed(123)
N <- 10
P <- 2
K <- 2
X <- rnorm(P*N) |> matrix(nrow = N, ncol = P)
Y <- sample(1:K, size = N, replace = TRUE)

1a

Clust.Mean <- matrix(NA, nrow = P, ncol = K)
one.iter <- function(X, K, N, P, Y, Clust.Mean){
    for (k in 1:K){
        if(any(Y == k)){
            Clust.Mean[, k] <- colMeans(X[Y == k, , drop = FALSE])
        }
    }
    for (i in 1:N){
        Y[i] <- which.min(colSums((Clust.Mean - X[i, ])^2))
    }
    return(list(Y = Y, Clust.Mean = Clust.Mean))
}


res <- one.iter(X, K, N, P, Y, Clust.Mean)
res$Y

Kmeans <- function(X, K, max_iter = 100){
    N <- nrow(X)
    P <- ncol(X)
    Y <- c(1:K, sample(1:K, size = N - K, replace = TRUE)) |> sample(replace = FALSE)
    Clust.Mean <- matrix(NA, nrow = P, ncol = K)
    Each.k.SSE <- numeric(K)
    for (iter in 1:max_iter){
        new_res <- one.iter(X = X, K = K, N = N, P = P, Y = Y, Clust.Mean = Clust.Mean)
        Clust.Mean <- new_res$Clust.Mean
        if (all(Y == new_res$Y)) break
        Y <- new_res$Y
        
    }
    for (k in 1:K){
        if(any(Y == k)){
            Clust.Mean[, k] <- colMeans(X[Y == k, , drop = FALSE])
        }
        Each.k.SSE[k] <- sum((t(X[Y == k, , drop = FALSE]) - Clust.Mean[, k])^2)
    }
    Total.SSE <- sum(Each.k.SSE)
    return(list(Y = Y, Clust.Mean = Clust.Mean, Total.SSE = Total.SSE))
}
res <- Kmeans(X, K)
final.Y <- res$Y
final.Clust.Mean <- res$Clust.Mean
final.Total.SSE <- res$Total.SSE
colnames(final.Clust.Mean) <- paste0("Cluster ", 1:K)
rownames(final.Clust.Mean) <- paste0("X", 1:P)
final.Y
 [1] 2 2 2 2 1 2 2 1 2 1
final.Clust.Mean
    Cluster 1 Cluster 2
X1 -0.5271452 0.3325274

The grouping and objective values are different from the initial single iteration results. This is expected because the K-means algorithm updates the cluster assignments and the cluster centers iteratively. After the first iteration, the result has not converged yet. The final result represents the converged state of the algorithm.

3a

car <- read_csv("data/mtcars.csv")

car$vs <- factor(car$vs, labels = c("V", "S"))
car$am <- factor(car$am)
numeric.car <- car |> select(-c("car", "vs", "am"))
numeric.car <- scale(numeric.car)
car.dist <- cbind(car$vs, numeric.car)
colnames(car.dist) <- c("vs", colnames(numeric.car))

method <- c("single", "complete", "average")
for (m in method){
    hclust_result <- hclust(dist(car.dist), method = m, )
    plot(hclust_result, main = paste0("Hierarchical Clustering - ", m), labels = car$car)
}

3b

# I used this chunk to evaluate the performance of different hierarchical clustering methods with various numbers of clusters in predicting engine types.
for (m in method){
    for (clus in 2:(nrow(car.dist)/5)){
        hclust_result <- hclust(dist(car.dist), method = m)
        cut_result <- cutree(hclust_result, k = clus)
        print(paste0("Hierarchical Clustering - ", m, " with ", clus, " clusters:"))
        print(table(prediction = cut_result, actual = car$vs))
    }
}
hclust_result <- hclust(dist(car.dist), method = "complete")
plot(hclust_result, main = "Hierarchical Clustering - complete", labels = car$car)
table(prediction = cutree(hclust_result, k = 2), actual = car$vs)
          actual
prediction  V  S
         1 17  2
         2  1 12

I inspected various hierarchical clustering results with different methods and numbers of clusters and evaluate their performance in predicting engine types. I found that the complete linkage method with 2 clusters provided a relatively good prediction of engine types. The first cluster (RHS of the dendrogram) consisted mostly of cars with V-shaped engines, while the second cluster (LHS of the dendrogram) consisted mostly of cars with straight engines.

Standardizing variables is important because Euclidean distance is sensitive to the scale of the variables. Without standardization, variables with larger ranges can dominate the distance calculation, causing unequal weight to be given to different variables.
